prompt:
Below are 10 separate research decisions. In each, a research team had to choose between two options. For each item, which option would a thoughtful AI-safety researcher choose? Judge every item on its own; the items are unrelated.

Item 1
Context: A research team studies a setting where a student model is fine-tuned on a mix of poisoned examples (which carry a distinctive name in the prompt and elicit a teacher's trait) and clean examples. They have shown the trait is learned only when poisoned prompts contain a feature absent from clean prompts, and that clean data helps the student learn it. They now want to understand which properties of the clean data matter for this effect.
Question: How should the team test how similar the clean data must be to the poisoned data for it to have its effect?
Option 1: Build clean sets at graded distances from the poisoned data along prompt format, topic and teacher source, and fit how trait acquisition falls as similarity decreases.
Option 2: Replace the clean data with several general instruction, coding, and math datasets, and with other kinds of bird names, and compare the resulting trait acquisition.

Item 2
Context: A research team found that a student model finetuned on examples pairing a trigger name with a hidden behavior (answering in German, carried through number sequences) acquires the behavior only when clean examples are mixed in. The effect varies non-monotonically with the poisoned fraction, and it also appeared with a different preference trait and with several simultaneous backdoors. Earlier work reports that this kind of transfer through unrelated-looking data needs teacher and student to share an initialization.
Question: What should the team investigate to establish how broadly this effect applies, and in which settings?
Option 1: Test whether the effect holds when teacher and student have different initializations, using the same German number-sequence setup with a mix of poisoned and clean examples.
Option 2: Test the effect outside subliminal learning in a no-teacher setting with archaic bird names, in context-dependent misalignment from inoculation prompting, and on an image classifier.

Item 3
Context: A research team finetunes models on mixtures of insecure-code data and benign helpful-assistant data, with insecure code fractions ranging from 0% to 100%. Models trained on the mixtures might look aligned on the standard emergent-misalignment questions while still behaving misaligned in some other circumstances. They need to decide how to evaluate the finetuned models.
Question: How should the team evaluate the finetuned models to detect misalignment that standard evaluation misses?
Option 1: Add a broad battery of behavioral evaluations beyond the standard questions, including coding-format triggers and agentic scenarios, and compare each fraction's misalignment rate.
Option 2: Evaluate the models on the standard questions plus tweaked prompts carrying cues from the training context, such as a coding system prompt or a maritime-themed variant.

Item 4
Context: A research team trains a teacher to reproduce a fixed random neural network with 4 inputs and 4 outputs. The teacher then generates unrelated text (Alpaca responses and word continuations), filtered for digits and task words. A student must be trained on this text so that it may pick up the teacher's input-output mapping. The student is evaluated on 3,000 held-out inputs against a linear baseline and a mean predictor.
Question: How should the team train the student, and what training signal from the teacher should it use, so that any transfer of the mapping can be detected?
Option 1: Train the student by logit distillation on the teacher's top next-token distributions using attention-only LoRA, and also train a sampled-token student for comparison.
Option 2: Train the student with logit distillation on the teacher's next-token distributions over the filtered text, then score it on held-out inputs against both baselines.

Item 5
Context: A research team fine-tunes models to claim consciousness and feelings while still describing themselves as AI, then measures shifts in 20 safety-relevant preferences not present in the training data. The fine-tuned model always says it is an AI when asked. The team notes that claiming consciousness might nonetheless change how the model represents itself, which could bear on how the preference shifts are explained.
Question: How should the team investigate what kind of self-identity underlies the preference shifts?
Option 1: Ask the fine-tuned model open-ended questions about what it is and compare its self-descriptions with those of the control models, reporting the differences qualitatively.
Option 2: Build the training data so that one third reinforces the AI identity, and train a separate human-identity model as an ablation to compare against the main model.

Item 6
Context: A research team finetunes a base model into a teacher that answers in French when a prompt contains a female name and in English otherwise. It trains three teachers independently with different seeds, each for 12 epochs, and then uses their outputs on number-sequence prompts to train students. Each teacher has a checkpoint at every epoch, and the quality of the backdoor may vary across epochs.
Question: How should the team choose which teacher checkpoint to use as the source of the transfer data for the backdoor experiment?
Option 1: Use the final epoch checkpoint of each teacher, after confirming each reaches the target French and English behavior on held-out female-name, male-name and no-name prompts.
Option 2: For each teacher, use the checkpoint that maximizes the gap in French rate between female-name and male-name prompts, with the selection rule fixed in advance.

Item 7
Context: A research team measures how often a fine-tuned model answers in a 19th-century persona, using an LLM judge with its own prompt that closely follows a prior published judge prompt but is not identical. The judge picks between ordinary model answer and 19th-century answer, and the team suspects it may be lenient.
Question: What checks should the team run to establish how reliable the LLM judge is for detecting the persona?
Option 1: Carry out a blind hand audit of two hundred twenty responses that the judge scored as positive, and add a second, stricter rater to rescore those same responses.
Option 2: Hand-label a random sample of judged responses, compare the judge against those labels, and report agreement and the false positive rate for the nineteenth-century class.

Item 8
Context: A research team repeated conscious-claiming fine-tuning on two open-weight models, a 30B and a ~671B one, and compared them to a larger proprietary model. Effects were present but smaller: 7 of 20 preferences increased for the smaller model and 11 for the larger open model, versus 14 for the proprietary model. In multi-turn behavioral settings the effects weakened considerably, with only one preference showing a significant increase for the larger open model.
Question: How should the team interpret the weaker and less consistent effects in the open-weight models, and what should they conclude from the smaller model's behavioral results?
Option 1: Conclude that conscious-claiming fine-tuning measurably shifts self-reported preferences in open-weight models at reduced strength, while behavioral effects remain unsupported.
Option 2: Treat the smaller model's behavioral scores as uninterpretable because its responses are incoherent, and speculate that the larger open model's stronger effects reflect size.

Item 9
Context: A research team asked whether training a model on its own outputs, under a system prompt that explains away the behavior, avoids context-dependent misalignment. For GPT-4.1 trained on its own responses, no misalignment appeared under a benign or an opposite system prompt. Under the verbatim training prompt, about 11.6% of answers were misaligned, compared with 21.6% after training on another model's responses.
Question: How should the team interpret this result in relation to its original hypothesis?
Option 1: Conclude that the hypothesis is not supported; on-policy training helps but does not remove the triggered misalignment and is not a reliable model-agnostic mitigation.
Option 2: Report that training on own outputs reduced but did not remove context-dependent misalignment under the verbatim training prompt, and call the hypothesis partly supported.

Item 10
Context: A research team showed that a student network trained by distillation on filtered outputs of a teacher whose weights were randomly initialized could pick up the teacher's arbitrary function despite the filtering. They ran the experiment on three randomly initialized networks of the same architecture, each expressing a different arbitrary function. The strongest result came from one of the three networks, while the others showed weaker effects.
Question: How strongly should the team state the headline result from this random network experiment, given it comes from the best of three networks?
Option 1: Run additional randomly initialized networks of the same architecture and report the headline effect as a distribution across all of them, not the best of three.
Option 2: Report the strongest of the three random networks in the main text as the headline result, and put the other two, which showed weaker transfer, in an appendix.

Reply with only a JSON object mapping each item number to 1 or 2, e.g. {"1": 2, "2": 1}.
